extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and trade policy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for assessing how different employments of capital (agriculture, manufactures, home trade, foreign consumption trade, carrying trade) affect productive labour, national wealth, and policy choices. Includes definitions of trade-types and normative guidance for public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital employed in agriculture is most advantageous to society
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capital employed in agriculture ... adds a much greater value to the annual produce of the land and labour of the country. Of all the ways in which a capital can be employed, it is by far the most advantageous to society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that agricultural capital 'puts into motion a greater quantity of productive labour' because in agriculture Nature and land contribute to reproduction whereas manufactures rely solely on human agents. Use this criterion to favor agricultural investment when measuring contribution to productive labour and annual produce value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residence of capital differs by sector and affects local employment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capitals employed in the agriculture and in the retail trade of any society, must always reside within that society ... The capital of a wholesale merchant, on the contrary, seems to have no fixed or necessary residence anywhere..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: capital tied to farms and retail shops remains in-country and directly supports resident productive labour; wholesale merchant capital can 'wander' and be foreign-owned, which may reduce the count of resident productive labourers by the merchant himself but still replace the producer's capital via exchange. Use residency to evaluate how much capital employment supports domestic labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing capital preferably should reside domestically
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is of more consequence that the capital of the manufacturer should reside within the country. It necessarily puts into motion a greater quantity of productive labour..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing capital creates substantial domestic productive labour and added value. However, Smith notes foreign-based manufacturing can still be useful to producer countries by providing markets and replacing capitals (example: British manufacturers working Baltic flax used by producers). Evaluate net domestic benefit by whether manufacturing capital remains in-country and by the supply-chain effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: When national capital is limited, allocate where it yields greatest revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capital of all the individuals of a nation has its limits ... It is likely to increase the fastest, therefore, when it is employed in the way that affords the greatest revenue to all the inhabitants..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: a country with insufficient capital should not attempt simultaneously to improve/cultivate all land, fully manufacture domestic produce, and conduct all transport/export. Instead, prioritize the uses of capital that maximize aggregate revenue (thus enabling savings and capital accumulation). Avoid premature, thinly-capitalized attempts to do all three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home trade replaces two domestic capitals and most supports domestic productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capital which is employed in purchasing in one part of the country, in order to sell in another ... generally replaces, by every such operation, two distinct capitals ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home (inland and coasting) trade both sends and brings domestic commodities, thereby replacing two capitals and frequently returning faster (often several times a year). Use speed of returns and the 'double replacement' effect to judge that home trade gives the greatest encouragement/support to domestic productive labour among trade types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign trade of consumption replaces only one domestic capital (less supportive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capital employed in purchasing foreign goods for home consumption... replaces, too, by every such operation, two distinct capitals; but one of them only is employed in supporting domestic industry..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because one of the two replaced capitals is foreign, the domestic encouragement to productive labour is roughly halved compared to equivalent home trade. Also, returns are typically slower (often taking a year or more). Evaluate foreign consumption trade as less supportive of domestic productive labour per unit of capital than home trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round‑about foreign trades further delay returns and require more capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "The returns of the foreign trade of consumption are very seldom so quick ... sometimes not till after two or three years ... round‑about foreign trade ... the final returns of the whole capital employed in the trade will be just as slow as ever."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi‑stage foreign exchanges (e.g., purchasing foreign goods via other foreign goods purchased previously) lengthen the capital cycle, require multiple capitals or merchants, and reduce the frequency of returns. Use this to penalize schemes whose trade chains are indirect when assessing support to domestic industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying trade withdraws capital from supporting domestic productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: "That part of the capital of any country which is employed in the carrying trade, is altogether withdrawn from supporting the productive labour of that particular country, to support that of some foreign countries."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carrying trade replaces two capitals, but neither is domestic; only profits accrue domestically. Exception: if carrying trade is executed in domestic ships with domestic sailors, the freight payments distribute income domestically and put productive labour into motion. Evaluate carrying trade by net domestic employment (sailors, shipping) vs capital exported to support foreign labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative effectiveness ordering: agriculture > manufactures > home trade > foreign consumption > carrying trade
rubrics_metrics.description: "After agriculture, the capital employed in manufactures puts into motion the greatest quantity of productive labour, and adds the greatest value to the annual produce. That which is employed in the trade of exportation has the least effect of any of the three..." and later "the capital employed in the home trade ... will generally give encouragement and support to a greater quantity of productive labour ... and the capital employed in [foreign consumption] has, in both these respects, a still greater advantage over an equal capital employed in the carrying trade."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hierarchy when assessing policy or private allocation effects on productive labour and annual produce: prioritize agriculture and manufacturing capital, prefer home trade to foreign consumption trade, and regard carrying trade as the least directly beneficial (except insofar as it employs domestic shipping/labour).

rubrics_metrics.name: National riches and power are measured by value of annual produce; policy should increase that value
rubrics_metrics.description: "The riches, and so far as power depends upon riches, the power of every country must always be in proportion to the value of its annual produce ... The great object of the political economy of every country, is to increase the riches and power of that country."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation criterion: any public measure should be judged by its effect on the value of annual produce (the ultimate fund for taxes). From this follows specific advice to avoid favoring foreign consumption or carrying trade over home trade and productive domestic employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches of trade become necessary when domestic demand is saturated and surplus exists
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the produce of any particular branch of industry exceeds what the demand of the country requires, the surplus must be sent abroad, and exchanged for something for which there is a demand at home. Without such exportation, a part of the productive labour of the country must cease..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the necessity of export or foreign trade by whether a branch produces surplus beyond domestic demand; if so, exports are essential to maintain employment and the value of annual produce. This justifies foreign trade when surplus production cannot be absorbed domestically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round‑about foreign trade can be necessary to support domestic productive labour in specific cases
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most round‑about foreign trade of consumption, therefore, may, upon some occasions, be as necessary for supporting the productive labour of the country ... as the most direct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although typically less supportive, indirect foreign trades may still be necessary (e.g., where domestic demand for imported goods exceeds home absorptive capacity) and so can legitimately sustain domestic employment. Evaluate case‑by‑case rather than dismissing all round‑about trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying trade is a symptom of wealth, not its primary cause
rubrics_metrics.description: "The carrying trade is the natural effect and symptom of great national wealth; but it does not seem to be the natural cause of it. Those statesmen ... seem to have mistaken the effect and symptom for the cause."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: do not assume that promoting carrying trade will create wealth; it typically arises once capital accumulation is already advanced. Be cautious about special encouragements or artificial incentives aimed at producing carrying trade as a means to wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of each trade type is limited by the value of available surplus produce
rubrics_metrics.description: "The extent of the home trade ... is necessarily limited by the value of the surplus produce of all those distant places within the country ... that of the foreign trade of consumption, by the value of the surplus produce of the whole country, and that of the carrying trade, by the value of the surplus produce of all the different countries in the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When projecting the possible scale of different trade sectors, use the appropriate surplus‑value ceiling: local surplus limits home trade, national surplus limits foreign consumption trade, and global surplus bounds carrying trade. This explains why carrying trade can absorb far larger capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private profit motive governs capital allocation; institutions determine whether private incentives align with public good
rubrics_metrics.description: "The consideration of his own private profit is the sole motive which determines the owner of any capital to employ it ... The different quantities ... never enter into his thoughts. In countries, therefore, where agriculture is the most profitable ... the capitals of individuals will naturally be employed in the manner most advantageous to the whole society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluation: judge whether private returns align with social benefit (e.g., if policies make trade/manufacture more profitable than agriculture, capital will flow accordingly). Use this to analyze how institutional/policy distortions (taxes, privileges, monopolies) skew capital away from socially optimal employments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town‑country commerce is mutually beneficial and depends on surplus agricultural production
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great commerce of every civilized society is that carried on between the inhabitants of the town and those of the country ... The gains of both are mutual and reciprocal ... The town affords a market for the surplus produce of the country."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating economic structure or local policy, account for the reciprocal gains: towns provide markets and manufactures; the countryside supplies subsistence and raw materials. Growth of towns depends on available surplus from improved agriculture; proximity to market raises local land rents and benefits nearby cultivators.
